transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-29 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Alex Chen, Priya Singh (Redwood)  Mark Davenport, Leah Ortiz, Samir Patel (Stratus Finance)

Summary: quick run-through of audit logs and admin activity. Focus on what is captured, how we export, retention and KMS onboarding. Customer asked about whether request payloads are retained and how to stream to Splunk/Datadog.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining  appreciate you carving out time today. Alex from Redwood, uh, AE here, with Priya from our SE team.
[00:08] Mark Davenport: Thanks Alex. I'm Mark, CISO at Stratus Finance. Leah and Samir are here from infra/sec. We're mostly focused on auditability and retention  especially around admin actions and any PII in logs.
[00:18] Leah Ortiz: Yeah, we want to make sure we can ingest these into our SIEM and meet our compliance windows.
[00:23] Priya Singh: Great, we'll go over the default capture surface, export options, and how encryption/KMS works. I'll try to call out differences between Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployments.
[00:32] Alex Chen: Quick agenda: capture, export, retention, integrity, and then open Q&A and next steps.

[02:05] Priya Singh: Starting with capture  audit logs capture admin-level activity: user logins (SSO events), role & permission changes, API key and token creation/deletion, service account activity, changes to routing/policies, model deploys and rollouts, config changes in the console, and targeted data access events.
[02:25] Samir Patel: When you say "targeted data access events" do you mean actual payloads of requests or just metadata?
[02:30] Priya Singh: Good question. By default we capture metadata: request ID, timestamp, user/principal, endpoint, model version, latency, token counts, and any high-level operation (e.g., create-completion, embeddings call). For hosted customers we do not persist full request bodies that contain raw user content unless customers opt into enhanced logging via a compliant ingestion flow  typically for POCs where the customer approves retention and redaction rules.
[02:58] Mark Davenport: So PII won't be stored in plain text in audit logs by default?
[03:02] Priya Singh: Correct. We avoid storing user prompt content in standard audit logs. We do store metadata that ties back to request IDs so you can correlate with redacted record stores if needed.

[05:10] Leah Ortiz: For SSO/SSO logout events, is the identity provider assertion logged?
[05:14] Priya Singh: We log the SAML/OIDC event (login success/failure), user id, provider, and timestamp. We don't retain the full assertion payload. You can configure whether to include additional headers in exported logs if you want more context.

[07:45] Alex Chen: On export options  we support S3 bucket delivery (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS), streaming syslog to a customer endpoint, Kafka, and direct SIEM integration through webhooks or our managed Splunk/Datadog forwarder.
[07:59] Samir Patel: Is the S3 export encrypted with our KMS CMK if we provide one?
[08:03] Priya Singh: Yes. For Private and Dedicated customers we support customer-managed keys (CMK) in AWS KMS  you can supply the key ARN. For Hosted, we offer either Redwood-managed KMS or an enterprise plan that supports BYOK (bring your own key) for audit logs.
[08:20] Mark Davenport: What's the delivery latency for S3 exports? Near real-time?
[08:24] Priya Singh: S3 export is near real-time with batches every 1-5 minutes depending on volume. Syslog/Kafka is near real-time with sub-second to few-seconds delivery. Webhook/SIEM forwarders attempt immediate delivery with retries and dead-lettering.

[10:02] Leah Ortiz: Format  is the export JSON lines? Schema?
[10:06] Priya Singh: Exports default to newline-delimited JSON (ndjson) with a documented schema. Each event includes event_type, event_id, timestamp, principal, resource, ip, request_id, and a free-text message and fields for associated metadata (model name/version, tokens). We'll share the schema.
[10:22] Alex Chen: We'll attach the audit-log-schema.json to the follow-up.

[12:15] Samir Patel: Retention  what are defaults and what's possible?
[12:19] Priya Singh: Hosted default retention for audit logs is 90 days. For Dedicated and Private customers you can configure longer retention  typical enterprise options are 1 year, 3 years, or custom retention. If you export logs to your S3, you control retention there indefinitely. We also offer an archival add-on for multi-year retention with WORM-style immutability for compliance.
[12:44] Mark Davenport: Is immutability verifiable?
[12:47] Priya Singh: We support append-only storage with write-once buckets (when using our archival add-on) and generate tamper-evident hashes and sequence numbers per batch. You can also opt into signed log entries where each log batch is cryptographically signed; we keep the signature chain and can provide proof of integrity.

[15:05] Leah Ortiz: How do you handle log integrity if we rotate keys?
[15:08] Priya Singh: Key rotation is supported  signatures include key version metadata. If using customer-managed KMS, rotations are performed per your KMS policies; signatures are rekeyed accordingly. We maintain a key registry mapping signatures to key versions for auditability.

[17:40] Alex Chen: On access controls to logs  RBAC in Redwood Console: you can restrict who can read audit logs, who can export, and who can configure retention. We integrate with SSO (SAML/SCIM) so you can sync group membership and enforce least privilege.
[17:58] Samir Patel: Does the export role require separate credentials?
[18:02] Priya Singh: Exports to customer S3 require an IAM role or presigned credentials depending on the chosen flow. For streaming to syslog/Kafka you provide an endpoint and auth token. We recommend using an IAM role with limited write permissions scoped to the export prefix.

[19:50] Mark Davenport: For incident forensics we need correlation between audit logs and raw requests  is there a way to map them reliably?
[19:56] Priya Singh: Yes, each request is given a canonical request_id that's included in metadata logs and in operational traces. If you opt into content retention for a given POC or with additional contractual controls, we can link request content to request_id for a defined retention period and redaction policy. Without that opt-in we only retain metadata to preserve privacy.

[22:30] Leah Ortiz: Can we stream directly into Splunk or do we need an intermediary?

[22:33] Priya Singh: We have native Splunk HEC support and a Datadog forwarder. You can also route via Kafka if you prefer. For Splunk we can push events into your HEC endpoint with auth token; events are in ndjson and Splunk sourcetypes are documented.

[24:10] Samir Patel: Any rate limits or cost implications for high-volume exports?
[24:14] Alex Chen: Exports are metered; high-volume streaming may incur additional charges, and we recommend batching and compression to reduce cost. We'll include estimated egress/throughput pricing in the follow-up.

[26:45] Mark Davenport: Regarding SOC2/ISO evidence  can you provide logs as part of the SOC2 audit package?
[26:50] Priya Singh: We can provide SOC 2 Type II reports and supplemental audit artifacts. For specific event-level evidence we can provide export samples and attestations, but final auditor access depends on your engagement model; for Dedicated/Private customers we can grant read-only access to a subset of logs for auditors under an NDA.

[29:05] Leah Ortiz: Are admin activity logs tamper-resistant in Hosted?
[29:09] Priya Singh: In Hosted we use encrypted, append-only stores and maintain signatures. For the highest assurance we recommend Dedicated with archival add-on and CMKs  that combination provides customer control over keys and immutable retention guarantees.

[31:55] Samir Patel: What about cross-region replication for residency? We have EU data-residency requirements.
[31:59] Priya Singh: We support region-scoped logging  audit logs for EU-region accounts are stored in EU regions by default. Exports to customer S3 can be to your regional bucket to meet residency rules. Cross-region replication is possible but would need to be explicitly enabled and documented for compliance.

[34:12] Mark Davenport: Any gotchas around forensic timestamps? Are timestamps normalized to UTC?
[34:16] Priya Singh: All timestamps are recorded in RFC3339 UTC and we include the originating service time and ingestion time. That helps with clock drift analysis.

[36:30] Leah Ortiz: We need a sample ndjson file and the schema to validate ingestion.
[36:34] Alex Chen: We'll share that. Priya, can you set up a temporary export to their test S3?
[36:39] Priya Singh: Yep. I'll provision a temp S3 export and send instructions  we'll use SSE-KMS and share the manifest and sample files.

[38:05] Mark Davenport: Ok  next steps from our side: confirm retention requirements and whether we want request content for a short POC.
[38:12] Samir Patel: We'll also validate SIEM ingestion.

[40:00] Alex Chen: Great, recap: Alex to send schema and SOC artifacts; Priya to enable temporary S3 export and provide onboarding steps; Stratus to confirm retention policy and whether to enable content retention for a time-boxed POC.
[40:12] Mark Davenport: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[40:18] Priya Singh: Thanks  we'll follow up with the links.
[40:22] Alex Chen: Bye all.

End of transcript.
